paras: The hanging of Henry Harvey was an attempted lynching at Chico, Wise County, Texas, in late January or early February 1888, in which a party of twelve men took a prisoner accused of burglary from his guard and hanged him twice. He was cut down alive and later reported in jail, and the episode drew local condemnation and a promised grand jury inquiry.

According to a dispatch from Decatur, the county seat, James Anderson and Henry Harvey were arrested at Chico on a charge of burglary. The constable set out for Decatur with Anderson and left Harvey under guard at Chico. A later report from Decatur named the three men guarding him as John R. McCracken, Deck Holden and Bill Largent.

Late at night a party of twelve men took Harvey from the guard and "strung him up twice." Harvey insisted he was innocent and asked for time to pray, after which, the dispatch said, he declared himself ready to die. After hanging for some time he was cut down "nearer dead than alive."

The first dispatch said the county authorities would investigate. On February 4 a Decatur correspondent of the Fort Worth Daily Gazette wrote that the earlier report was "literally true" and that the act was condemned by "the good people of the Chico country," which he described as the most law-abiding part of the county. He said no blame attached to the guards, that the grand jury would meet on Monday to investigate, and that the prisoner and Anderson were both in jail on a complaint of theft and burglary. No report of the grand jury's findings or of any arrest of the twelve men appears in the coverage.

The Decatur dispatch ran by wire on February 3 and 4 in papers from Washington and Alexandria to St. Paul, Memphis, Camden and Waterbury, and in Kansas weeklies the following week. Its headlines varied widely: the Evening Star used "Torturing a Prisoner in Texas" and the St. Paul Daily Globe "Disgraceful Proceedings," while the Memphis Appeal ran "A Burglar's Narrow Escape" and Kansas papers "One Way to Make Him Tell." Several of these framed the hanging as a way of forcing a confession, and the Alexandria Gazette called it an "Attempt to Lynch."

Shorter versions appeared among condensed telegrams, and one in the Springfield Daily Republic of Ohio stated flatly that Harvey, "a burglar," had been lynched. The Fort Worth Daily Gazette's local follow-up differed in tone, deploring "mob law and summary justice" while defending the guards and the neighborhood's reputation. No report names the race of the prisoner or of the men who hanged him.

The wire called the prisoner Henry Harvey, while the Gazette correspondent called him Joe Hovey; both place him at Chico with Anderson, and the Gazette presented its report as confirming the earlier one. The dates also differ: the Gazette put the hanging on Tuesday night, January 31, while the wire, dated February 3, described an arrest "yesterday" and a hanging late "last night." Only the one-line Ohio brief reported a death; the full dispatch and the later local report both have him alive.

reader.title: Hanging of Henry Harvey at Chico, Texas
bases: A party of twelve men took an accused burglar from his guards and hanged him twice before cutting him down alive, an attempted lynching (A1, A9).

Twelve men with no lawful authority seized and hanged a man accused of burglary, but the full wire says he was cut down alive and the local Gazette report places him in jail afterward (A1, A9); a one-line Ohio brief saying he 'was lynched' is a condensation of the same wire and is outweighed (A3).

The Decatur wire (A1) and a separate local Decatur special to the Fort Worth Gazette that confirms it as 'literally true' (A9) agree on the core event, although they differ on the victim's name and the date.

accounts.label: Decatur wire
accounts.gist: Anderson and Harvey were arrested at Chico for burglary; while the constable took Anderson to Decatur, twelve men took Harvey from his guard, strung him up twice and cut him down nearly dead; he protested his innocence and asked time to pray.

accounts.label: Fort Worth Gazette Decatur correspondent
accounts.gist: Confirmed the earlier report as 'literally true', called the victim Joe Hovey, dated it Tuesday night, cleared the three guards, and said the grand jury would investigate.

accounts.label: Ohio condensed telegram
accounts.gist: Reported in one line that Harvey, 'a burglar', had been lynched.

framing.detail: Wire headlines ranged from 'Torturing a Prisoner in Texas' and 'Disgraceful Proceedings' to the lighter 'One Way to Make Him Tell' and 'A Burglar's Narrow Escape'.
The Fort Worth Gazette's correspondent wrote that the neighborhood looked 'with horror upon mob law and summary justice' while defending the guards.
Most papers ran the Decatur dispatch nearly verbatim, some as one-line telegrams.

conflicts.note: Both reports pair him with James Anderson / Anderson and place the event at Chico, so they describe the same man.
